title: Upper Density and Positive Upper Density
content: Defines the upper density of A as the limsup of |A ∩ [1,N]| / N as N → ∞. A set has positive upper density if this quantity exceeds 0. These definitions are restated from the parent for import independence.
mathContext: $\bar{d}(A) = \limsup_{N \to \infty} \frac{|A \cap [1,N]|}{N}$. A set has positive upper density if $\bar{d}(A) > 0$.

title: Sumset Operation B +_s C
content: The sumset B + C = {b + c : b ∈ B, c ∈ C}, defined as a set comprehension with custom notation +_s. This is the central object of the Erdős sumset conjecture.
mathContext: $B + C = \{b + c : b \in B, c \in C\}$. Also called the Minkowski sum in geometry.

title: Syndetic Sets (Bounded Gaps)
content: A set S is syndetic if there exists a bound g such that every interval [n, n+g] contains an element of S. Syndetic sets have uniformly bounded gaps and arise naturally in topological dynamics.
mathContext: $S$ is syndetic if $\exists g \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, S \cap [n, n+g] \neq \emptyset$. Equivalently, the gap sequence $\sup_{n} \min\{s \in S : s \geq n\} - n$ is bounded.

title: Thick Sets (Arbitrarily Long Runs)
content: A set S is thick if for every g, there exists an interval [n, n+g] entirely contained in S. Thick sets are the dual of syndetic sets: S is thick iff S intersects every syndetic set.
mathContext: $S$ is thick if $\forall g \in \mathbb{N}, \exists n, [n, n+g] \subseteq S$. Duality: $S$ is thick $\Leftrightarrow$ $S$ meets every syndetic set.

title: Piecewise Syndetic Sets
content: A set is piecewise syndetic if it is the intersection of a syndetic set and a thick set — equivalently, it has bounded gaps along arbitrarily long intervals. The theorem that positive density implies piecewise syndetic is stated but left as sorry (requires pigeonhole).
mathContext: $S$ is piecewise syndetic if $\exists T$ syndetic such that $S \cap T$ is thick. This is equivalent to: $\exists g, \forall L, \exists n, |S \cap [n, n+L]|$ has gaps $\leq g$.

title: Syndetic Sets Are Infinite
content: Proves that syndetic sets are infinite by showing they are unbounded: for every n, the syndetic condition provides an element m ≥ n in S. Uses Set.infinite_of_not_bddAbove.
mathContext: If $S$ is syndetic with gap bound $g$, then $\forall n, \exists m \in S$ with $m \geq n$, so $S$ is unbounded and hence infinite.

title: Gap-Controlled Sumset Conjecture
content: States the strengthened sumset conjecture: for any set A of positive upper density and any gap function f, there exist infinite B, C with B + C ⊆ A and consecutive elements of B separated by at least f(b). This was proved by Moreira-Richter-Robertson (2019).
mathContext: $\forall A$ with $\bar{d}(A) > 0$, $\forall f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^+$, $\exists B, C$ infinite with $B + C \subseteq A$ and $b_2 - b_1 \geq f(b_1)$ for consecutive $b_1 < b_2 \in B$.

title: Syndetic Sumset Question (Open)
content: States the open question: can B in the sumset decomposition B + C ⊆ A always be chosen to be syndetic? The formalization notes this is likely false — if A has large gaps, then B + C ⊆ A forces B and C to respect those gaps.
mathContext: $\forall A$ with $\bar{d}(A) > 0$, $\exists B$ syndetic, $C$ infinite, $B + C \subseteq A$? Likely FALSE in general.

title: IP Sets and Hindman's Theorem
content: Defines IP sets as sets containing all finite sums FS(x_1, x_2, ...) from some positive, strictly monotone sequence. Axiomatizes Hindman's theorem (1974): every finite coloring of N has a monochromatic IP set. This is one of the deepest results in Ramsey theory.
mathContext: $S$ is IP if $\exists (x_i)_{i \geq 0}$ with $x_i > 0$, $x_i$ strictly increasing, and $\mathrm{FS}(x_0, x_1, \ldots) = \{\sum_{i \in F} x_i : F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \text{ finite, nonempty}\} \subseteq S$. Hindman: $\forall k$-coloring of $\mathbb{N}$, $\exists$ monochromatic IP set.

title: Correction: Positive Density Does Not Imply IP
content: Documents a corrected mathematical error: a set of positive upper density need NOT contain an IP set. The counterexample is A = {n : n mod 3 ≠ 0}, which has density 2/3 but no IP subset (any IP set eventually contains elements summing to a multiple of 3). The correct relationship is IP*: positive density implies A intersects every IP set.
mathContext: $A = \{n : n \not\equiv 0 \pmod{3}\}$ has $\bar{d}(A) = 2/3$ but no IP subset. For any generators $x_1, x_2, \ldots$, if $x_1 \equiv x_2 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, then $x_1 + x_2 \equiv 2$ and $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$.

title: IP Sets Contain Infinite Sumsets (Odd/Even Splitting)
content: The main constructive result: every IP set S contains infinite sets B, C with B + C ⊆ S. The proof splits the generating sequence into odd-indexed (B) and even-indexed (C) subsequences. Both are infinite (by strict monotonicity), and their sums land in S because odd and even index sets are disjoint, so the union is a valid finite subset.
mathContext: Given $\mathrm{FS}(x_0, x_1, \ldots) \subseteq S$, let $B = \mathrm{FS}(x_1, x_3, x_5, \ldots)$ and $C = \mathrm{FS}(x_0, x_2, x_4, \ldots)$. For $b \in B, c \in C$: $b + c = \sum_{i \in F_{\text{odd}}} x_i + \sum_{j \in G_{\text{even}}} x_j = \sum_{k \in F_{\text{odd}} \cup G_{\text{even}}} x_k \in S$ since $F_{\text{odd}} \cap G_{\text{even}} = \emptyset$.

title: IP Sets Are Infinite
content: Proves IP sets are infinite by showing the generating sequence provides unbounded elements: x(k) ≥ k + 1 by induction on strict monotonicity, so each singleton sum x(k) gives an element of S exceeding k.
mathContext: If $(x_i)$ is strictly monotone with $x_0 \geq 1$, then $x_k \geq k + 1$ by induction, so $\{x_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\} \subseteq S$ is unbounded.

title: Hindman's Theorem for 2-Colorings
content: Applies Hindman's theorem to a 2-coloring of N: either A or its complement A^c contains an IP set. The proof constructs the coloring (0 if n ∈ A, 1 otherwise), applies the axiom, and case-splits on which color class wins.
mathContext: For any $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, either $A$ or $A^c$ contains an IP set. This follows from Hindman's theorem with $k = 2$.

title: Sumset Subset Characterization
content: A simple but useful equivalence: B + C ⊆ A if and only if for every b ∈ B and c ∈ C, b + c ∈ A. The proof is a direct unfolding of the sumset definition.
mathContext: $(B + C) \subseteq A \Leftrightarrow \forall b \in B, \forall c \in C, b + c \in A$.
